title: The d4 break and the typical middlegame structures
outcomes: Asks the three questions before a central break (can a pawn retake, is any piece or pawn loose, does a capture on e4 win anything) as a checklist, and says which one a given position fails
Tells a ready d4 from a premature one in positions that differ by one feature (the pawn on c3, a pawn attacking the bishop, a move on the other wing)
Names the block moves against the check on b4, says what each leaves, and knows why the pinned knight on c3 is playable but double-edged
Describes the isolated-pawn structure (what it gives White and what it costs), and counts the attackers and defenders of the pawn on d4

Describes the big-centre and closed-centre structures with one plan for each side, and avoids the typical mistakes (the e-pawn push once ...d5 attacks the bishop on c4, castling with the bishop attacked by a pawn, the knight recapture on d4)
Quotes our counts for move 5, 6 and 7 with their sample sizes and says what the counts do and do not show

steps.chapter: Hook: the pawn on c3 can take back
steps.caption: Move 6 of the Giuoco Piano, White to move. White pushed the d-pawn and Black took it. The pawn on c3 can take back, which would put two pawns side by side in the centre. Before any explanation, ask: if the pawn takes back, what will Black's bishop on c5 do with the new pawn, and what does White get in return?

steps.prompt: Your guess before any explanation, even if you are unsure: if White takes back with the c-pawn, what does the black bishop do next, and who gains from that? One sentence each.

steps.text: **The question of this lesson.** The pawn break d4 decides what kind of game an Italian becomes. Today you answer three questions: when does the break work, what structures follow it, and what is each side trying to do in each of them? By the end you can look at a pawn on c3 and a bishop on c4 and say which of three kinds of position is coming, and what you want from it.

steps.caption: Step through the recapture and Black's check. Count what each side has at the end: two white pawns abreast in the centre, against one tempo and a trade of bishops.

line.say: The c-pawn takes back. White now has two pawns side by side on d4 and e4, and the bishop on c4 still aims at f7.
Black's bishop gives check along the diagonal to e1. The check forces White to respond, but the exchange that follows also develops a white knight. [I] It is not clear that Black gains a tempo.

steps.caption: White is in check from the bishop on b4, and the knight on f6 attacks the pawn on e4. Seven moves answer the check. Good: the bishop or the b1 knight blocks on d2. Playable at a small cost: the knight block on c3 (it is pinned) and the king step to f1 (castling is lost). Bad: the king step to e2 and the f3 knight to d2. The queen block loses the queen at once. Which block would you choose, and what does it do about e4?

steps.text: **Three questions before the break.** First: when the pawn on d4 is taken, can a pawn take back? Second: is any of my pieces attacked by a pawn or left without a defender? Third: does the check, or the knight's attack on e4, win something? [I] This is a checklist, not a law: calm answers make the break probably playable. The next three positions change one feature each. Predict first.

steps.caption: Position 1: the break d4 in the position you know. Answer the three questions. Can a pawn retake? Is anything loose? What does the knight on f6 do to e4? Only one white unit is loose here, the pawn on e4, and that turns out to be affordable.

Only the pawn on e4 is attacked and undefended.
At depth 16 the engine's best move is d3 or the break d4, and d4 is within 40 centipawns of it.

steps.text: **The idea: a break is a question of timing.** The same pawn move is good in one position and loses a piece in the next. [I] A loose pawn on e4 matters only if Black's capture there wins something, or wins it with a gain of time. Two repairs appear: a knight on d2 guards the pawn, or White lets it go and wins the material back by a tactic.

steps.text: **What the isolated pawn means.** The pawn on d4 has no pawn beside it, so only pieces can guard it, and a black knight can sit on d5 where no pawn will ever chase it. In return White gets open lines for the rooks and the bishop. Capablanca (Chess Fundamentals, his ninth game) treated such a pawn as a target to attack from the start, trading minor pieces towards an ending [V-sheet]. [I] Engines are kinder to its owner: activity can pay for the weakness.

steps.text: **Structure A: the centre stands.** If Black does not strike back, White keeps both centre pawns. Pawns side by side attack four squares in Black's half, and Capablanca called such a pair the strongest centre, with a warning that pushing one to the fifth rank is a big decision [V-sheet]. [I] White's danger is impatience: the pawns are strongest when the pieces are developed first. Black is cramped but not lost; the next boards show what each side does.

steps.text: **Plans and warnings in structure A.** White: advance with tempo only when the pieces are ready, keep a rook behind the e-pawn, and use the space to attack the king or the weak squares. Black: undermine the advanced pawn with the c-pawn, trade pieces to relieve the cramp, and strike with the d-pawn when it is safe. [H] Many club losses here come from an unprepared push of the e-pawn, a hypothesis our data could test. The next board shows that push.

steps.text: **Structure C: the push.** White can answer the capture by pushing the e-pawn, attacking the knight. Black counters with a pawn strike of its own and the centre closes: White's pawns on d4 and e5 face Black's pawn on d5, like the pawn structure of the French Defence. Closed centres reward manoeuvres, and two things matter: strong squares for knights, and the bishop pair. [I] Plans, not calculation, decide these games.
